Separately, a name in the script, ʔEten, has no entry in config/pronunciations.json, so the text-to-speech engine guessed at its pronunciation. Add the entry before the next run that names it.

The roundup opened on local news and cut 21 stories

The pool is designed to be larger than one segment can air, so the cut is expected; the dropped stories can return on a day that matches them better. The roundup aired 5 local stories against 4 available, and it opened with local news. Nothing was split across subjects.

Of the 18 pooled stories, 12 of 18 roundup citations matched their sources. Of the 4 deep dives, 3 of 4 citations matched.

This is a script-level overlap the polish pass did not remove.

The local-first opening is the designed behaviour, and the cut stories remain in the pool for a later day. Four held articles never aired on their focus day

Focus routing released 0 articles and held 4. Two were held for "The Living World" and two for "Maker & Repair", with target release dates of 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-22. None of the four reached an episode on this run. They remain in the queue for their focus days, so the cost to listeners tonight was zero stories from those focus slots, and the cost to the cycle is that the Maker & Repair and Living World weeks will carry a smaller pool than the schedule assumes.

The forestry focus week (cycle week 2 of 4) released nothing from the focus routing itself, so the theme and local material carried the whole episode. Check whether the routing should release a minimum count when the focus day is not the current one.

Eighteen roundup stories kept, twenty-three cut, two deep dives

The roundup pool held 18 stories: 15 theme and 3 local. The airtime budget (NEWS_ROUNDUP_COUNT) dropped 23 from the pool, so the aired segment covered a fraction of what was curated. By design, the cut stories stay eligible for a later day. The deep dive pair was the Quesnel curtailment coverage, with the lead set to local under the Cariboo heading, which is where the debate question on who counts as affected by the curtailment came from.

Of 5 local stories available, 3 aired, and the roundup opened on local material. Citation alignment in the roundup matched 11 of 18, while both deep-dive citations matched. The gap in the roundup is the one to watch: 7 unmatched citations in a segment of 15 planned pairs means some spoken claims are not tied to a source the listener can find.

Change: review the roundup citation matching in the script-assembly step, since 11 of 18 is the weakest number on the page.

The first draft came in 753 words short and the expand pass fixed it

The first draft ran 2547 words against a target of 3400. It was sent back for one expand pass and shipped at 3223 words, which is still under target. Under the rule that a thin day is intended and only matters against SHORT_EPISODE_WORDS, this run is acceptable, but the gap shows the pool was not deep enough to fill the target without the expand pass. Casey's share of the deep-dive words was 48%, and the Casey-to-Riley voice ratio was 0.92, so the two voices stayed close to balanced.

Two TTS takes came back shorter than their word count predicted. Each was retried once, and both retries stayed short. The longer take of each was kept, so no words were dropped from the audio, though the two takes may have been clipped at the source.

Change: if the expand pass is the regular fix for thin days, raise the default pool size so the first draft reaches target without a second pass.

Paz Rodríguez woke up about 5am at her home in Milpa Alta, a suburb of Mexico City, on 20 March 2021. She thought about her plans for the day: pick up yellow lilies and cacti from her mother’s house and sell them in the market. She reached for her phone, which was flooded with texts from her sister, Oliviera Rodríguez. “Mum’s dog is barking a lot,” she had written. “I keep calling and she won’t respond.”

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
items.content_html:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

items.title: [euronews.com] Five EU states plan Rwanda hub for rejected asylum seekers
items.content_html: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a plan in Vienna to transfer some migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected after final review to a return hub in Rwanda, the first such EU facility outside the bloc. The governments say the scheme would comply with EU and international law. The pilot is expected to cover about 100 to 200 people, with the first transfers planned for 2027. The countries argue that sending people to a third country when their country of origin will not take them back could increase removals and deter irregular migration. The proposed facilities would be open, but migrants could remain in Rwanda indefinitely if they cannot be returned to their home countries. Rights groups and legal experts warn that the plan could expose migrants to abuse and leave them without clear ways to challenge decisions. The 2023 UK Supreme Court ruling against a similar Rwanda arrangement provides a legal precedent. The five states are expected to work out detailed terms in early 2027 before launching the pilot later that year.

items.title: [news.err.ee] Estonia announces closure of three Russia crossings used by pedestrians and freight
items.content_html: Estonia plans to close its three remaining road crossings with Russia on Dec. 1, ending pedestrian and freight traffic at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula. The crossings are among the few land links still operating between Russia and the European Union since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Moscow suspended vehicle traffic at Narva in February 2024, but pedestrians continued to cross. The decision follows an attempted arson and explosion at Threod Systems, an Estonian maker of reconnaissance and attack drones in Viimsi, near Tallinn. Estonia says Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU, ordered the attack. Eight residents of Latvia were detained; authorities said company security stopped the attempt before it caused significant damage or injuries. How long the closure will last remains undecided. Interior Minister Igor Taro said Estonian ministers would decide whether it is temporary or indefinite. People from Estonia who are in Russia, along with truck drivers, have been given about two weeks to return before crossing becomes more difficult. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna was also due to raise possible new sanctions at an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Brussels on Monday, Nov. 16.

items.title: [channelnewsasia.com] ASEAN keeps Myanmar leaders barred, ties return to peace-plan progress
items.content_html: Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Nov. 15 to maintain restrictions on Myanmar’s political leaders’ participation in Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summits and foreign ministers’ meetings, and set conditions for their return. A career diplomat from Myanmar’s foreign ministry represented the country at the Manila summit, rather than its military-backed president or foreign minister. The leaders said restoring full political representation would depend on “sustained and concrete progress” on ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus, the bloc’s plan to end violence and advance dialogue, mediation and humanitarian aid. They called on the military, security forces and armed groups to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and pressed for a nationwide ceasefire and safe aid access. The leaders acknowledged that implementation remains insufficient; Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cited ongoing bombings and displacement. The statement also encouraged ASEAN members to engage Myanmar individually, in consultation with the bloc’s chair, while keeping the consensus as the main framework. Leaders did not decide in Manila when Myanmar could return to high-level political meetings; the question is expected to pass to Singapore when it assumes ASEAN’s rotating chair in 2027.
